The spotted notothen, Trematomus nicolai, exhibits several distinctive life history traits that reflect its adaptation to the stable, frigid conditions of the Southern Ocean. Field surveys of this benthic nototheniid have documented that individuals ultimately attain a maximum total length of 36 cm [Li = 36 cm], a size that places it among the mid-range of its genus. The species reaches its total length at puberty at 22.95 cm [Lp = 22.95 cm], based on comparative morphometric analyses with its congener Trematomus eulepidotus, a value that suggests a relatively delayed onset of reproductive maturation relative to its ultimate size. This length-based maturity threshold is consistent with the life history strategies observed in other slow-growing, high-latitude notothenioids, where sustained cold temperatures decouple growth rates from chronological age. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from length-weight regressions, is estimated at 147.3 grams [Wwp = 147.3 grams], marking the mass at which gonadal recrudescence typically begins in this species.

Reproductive output in Trematomus nicolai appears to be tightly constrained by the thermal regime of its habitat. Under the stable near-freezing conditions of McMurdo Sound, at temperatures averaging -1.4 °C [T = -1.4 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate for this species has been recorded at approximately 24.4 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 24.4 eggs per day]. This figure, equivalent to over 8900 eggs per year, represents a substantial fecundity that is characteristic of many demersal-spawning nototheniids. The egg production rate is likely sustained by the prolonged provisioning window made possible by the slow metabolic demands imposed by the polar environment. The extraordinary longevity of this species, also recorded at -1.4 °C [T = -1.4 °C], has been estimated from otolith annuli at 6935 days [am = 6935 days], or approximately 19 years, a lifespan that allows for multiple reproductive bouts across a prolonged adult phase.

The early developmental stages of Trematomus nicolai are marked by a reliance on fixed temperature regimes for successful embryogenesis. When incubating eggs were maintained in the laboratory at a constant temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C], the time required for complete embryonic development from fertilisation to hatching was observed to be 66 days [ab = 66 days]. This duration is notably longer than that recorded for some temperate nototheniid species incubated at similar temperatures, suggesting a slower developmental pace that may be linked to the species' comparatively large egg size. Following eclosion, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a minute mass that reflects the substantial maternal investment in yolk provisions relative to the small larval body. This hatchling mass is consistent with the recorded egg diameter of approximately 2.0 mm.

As individuals transition beyond the larval phase, somatic growth proceeds steadily towards a large adult body size. The ultimate wet weight for the species, derived from length-weight relationships, reaches 624.8 grams [Wwi = 624.8 grams]. This asymptotic body mass of approximately six hundred twenty-five grams is among the larger values reported for the benthic Trematomus species, likely facilitated by a diet dominated by infaunal polychaetes and small amphipods. The wet weight at which gonadal maturation commences has been estimated at 147.3 grams [Wwp = 147.3 grams], representing roughly twenty-four percent of the ultimate body mass, a proportional threshold common among iteroparous, slow-growing teleosts. This substantial investment in somatic growth prior to reproductive maturity ensures that individuals of Trematomus nicolai are of sufficient size to defend territories and allocate energy efficiently to successive spawning events across their long lifespans.

Comparative studies among congeneric nototheniids have highlighted the life history position of Trematomus nicolai as an intermediate strategist. While its total length at puberty of 22.95 cm [Lp = 22.95 cm] is similar to that of Trematomus eulepidotus, its ultimate total length of 36 cm [Li = 36 cm] is comparatively larger, suggesting a more extended growth trajectory that continues well after the onset of sexual maturity. The species demonstrates a classic trade-off between fecundity and longevity, as its maximum recorded lifespan of 6935 days [am = 6935 days] is accompanied by a substantial daily egg output of 24.4 eggs per day [Ri = 24.4 eggs per day] under its native thermal regime of -1.4 °C [T = -1.4 °C]. In contrast, the brief but critical egg incubation period of 66 days [ab = 66 days] at 0 °C [T = 0 °C] underlines the temperature-sensitivity of its early life history. This combination of protracted growth, considerable longevity, and high fecundity underscores the adaptation of Trematomus nicolai to a stable but resource-limited polar ecosystem.
